clinicalPearls: Any route of corticosteroid delivery can raise intraocular pressure, including topical eye drops, periocular and intravitreal injections, inhaled, nasal, dermatological and systemic preparations.
The angle is open and the clinical picture otherwise resembles primary open-angle glaucoma, so a medication history is essential.
Response usually develops within weeks of starting topical steroid, but potent intravitreal depots can cause a delayed and prolonged rise.

Around a third of the general population are moderate responders and a smaller proportion are high responders; primary open-angle glaucoma patients and their relatives respond more frequently and more strongly.
Children, particularly young ones, can respond rapidly and severely, sometimes within days.
Drop potency matters: more potent molecules cause larger rises, whereas weaker or ester-based steroids and some newer agents carry a lower risk.
The mainstay of management is stopping or reducing the steroid, or switching to a lower-potency agent, alongside pressure-lowering therapy.
Pressure usually normalises after topical steroid withdrawal, but an intravitreal depot may require surgical removal or filtration surgery if the effect persists.
reference.pathophysiology: Corticosteroids reduce aqueous outflow facility at the trabecular meshwork through several interacting mechanisms. They promote accumulation of extracellular matrix material, including glycosaminoglycans, fibronectin and cross-linked actin networks, within the juxtacanalicular meshwork, and they suppress the normal turnover of this matrix by reducing phagocytic activity and matrix metalloproteinase expression in trabecular cells. Changes in trabecular cell cytoskeleton and gene expression, including induction of myocilin, further stiffen the outflow pathway. The net effect is increased resistance to aqueous drainage through an anatomically open angle, raising intraocular pressure. Susceptibility is partly genetically determined, which parallels the shared predisposition seen in primary open-angle glaucoma.

normal-tension glaucoma with incidental steroid use
additionalInvestigations: detailed corticosteroid exposure history across all routes
intraocular pressure measurement and comparison with pre-treatment baseline
optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell complex
review for a periocular or intravitreal steroid depot on examination or imaging
redFlags: markedly raised pressure in a child on corticosteroids
persistent high pressure after an intravitreal steroid depot
glaucomatous optic nerve damage discovered at first presentation
very high pressures threatening rapid field loss in a known high responder
reference.prognosis: When recognised early and the steroid is withdrawn, intraocular pressure usually returns to normal without lasting damage; prolonged unrecognised elevation, or an inescapable long-acting depot, can produce permanent glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about non-ophthalmic steroids such as inhalers, nasal sprays and skin creams.
Continuing potent topical steroid for chronic conditions without monitoring pressure.
Assuming pressure will fall quickly after an intravitreal depot when the effect can persist for months.
Overlooking the heightened and rapid susceptibility of children.
Attributing the raised pressure solely to steroids in a uveitic eye where inflammation also contributes.

management: Withdraw or reduce the offending corticosteroid, or switch to the least potent effective preparation such as loteprednol or fluorometholone
Where steroid is unavoidable, lower intraocular pressure with topical agents: prostaglandin analogues, beta-blockers, alpha-agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
Surgical removal of an intravitreal steroid depot when pressure remains uncontrolled
Laser trabeculoplasty or filtration/drainage surgery for refractory pressure elevation
Monitor intraocular pressure, optic disc, OCT nerve-fibre layer and visual fields for glaucomatous progression
Identify steroid responders and check baseline and serial pressures whenever corticosteroids of any route are prescribed
Educate the patient and prescribers to avoid inadvertent continued steroid exposure across all delivery routes
